newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr gains as yen runs into selling.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr gains as yen runs into selling.

text.p: The Australian dollar ended the day pressing against resistance at US$0.7925/30, but was unable as yet to make a decisive break higher, traders said.

Buying against the yen and a firmer U.S. dollar in Asian trade helped the Australian dollar's cause but it still remained well inside the US$0.7855-0.7965 range in which it has spent the last month, traders said.
By 4.30 p.m. (0630 GMT) the Australian dollar was trading at US$0.7925/30, having traded to a high of US$0.7934/39 late in the day. It had started at US$0.7909/14 from US$0.7907/12 late on Monday.

"There's been a bit of Aussie/yen go through this morning and this afternoon, four or five lots," one trader said. While there were rumours the buying was associated with a samurai issue of about A$300 million, no issue had been announced by late Tuesday.
The buying against the yen saw the Australian dollar rise to 88.71/81 in late trading from an early 88.29/39 yen and a Monday close of 88.30/40.
Traders said there was selling from offshore as the unit approached 88.50 yen intially, including from some of those who had been good buyers of the dollar in the past.

"There's reasonable volume ... good two way interest from Tokyo," the trader said. "One of the good samurai players had been on the other side today," the trader said, but added the player had been absent as the unit moved above US$0.7920
The firmer tone saw the Australian dollar also finish firmer in trade weighted terms at 58.6, up from an opening 58.5 and a previous close of 58.4.

The U.S. dollar was also firmer in Asian trade, rising to near 112 yen, and over 1.53 marks, a tone that helped the local unit on the day. Other currencies to benefit against the yen were the mark and sterling, traders said.
Sterling also hit a fresh 11-month high of US$1.5827 in Asian trading, dealers said.

The New Zealand dollar, after looking like challenging its 8-1/2 year high of US$0.7025 early on, was dented by a better than expected inflation result, and then comments from NZ First leader Winston Peters, who holds the balance of power as negotiations continue to form a coalition government in NZ.

Peters said the NZ dollar was clearly too high for exporters, and that he had not decided on which party he would form a coalition with. He also said it would not necessarily be a bad thing if coalition talks continued until Christmas.
The NZ dollar ended at US$0.6962/67, after being above US$0.7000 in overnight and early trading.
For Australian markets the release of the Reserve Bank of Australia bulletin, containing the RBA's quarterly assessment on the economy and its prospects, is the key event for Wednesday.

The bulletin will give some idea of the RBA's thinking on the economy and monetary policy. While a 50 basis point rate cut is factored into the dollar market, in the bills market March futures traded to 68 points under the 7.0 percent official cash rate, implying that some were expecting more than one cut.

While any indication from the RBA of more than one cut may be a negative for the dollar by implying that the interest differential would narrow further than the market had expected, traders said any sign that the RBA has a reasonably upbeat outlook for the economy could be a positive for the dollar.
